timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm Eric Glademake. I'm from Studio Ediclademake from the Netherlands. We're presenting our
my stadium chair for the first time. If you see a mushroom, it's only actually the flower,
actually of the mushroom. So the stadium, that's actually the whole root structure of the
whole fungi which is underground. And that's for us the most interesting material. We had a kind
of fascination for this 3D printing movement. And we adapted a 3D printer and made a kind of
way to to print straw injected with this mycelium, this mushroom, it's only like plain straw. So
it's grounded, it's like powder. We infuse the mushroom because the mushroom apparently likes this
kind of straw to grow on. By infusing this mushroom, it works as a kind of clue. So it
pulls all these straw parts together. And as soon as you dry it, you get a kind of core material,
which is all bounded together. PLA is bioplastic and is commonly used in 3D printing.
In our research, we also investigated that. So it does a mushroom grow on PLA. Can it really
become one with it? In the end, out of our material research, where we ended up with was to print PLA
as a kind of outside cover and then fill it up with the straw. But we found a way to 3D printed.
The mycelium is all the way through the material and it pushes itself in its boundaries what we
created by modeling 3D shapes. So it becomes like a strong solid material. When we first printed,
it's actually quite happy because we, the straw, we put a lot of water in it. It was around 9 kilos
and now it only remains around 1. The mushrooms you see, which are popping out, they're more decorative.
Our main purpose was to find this combination between the robots, actually, or the machine and nature.
And to have these two work together to create a kind of new material, which could be applicable for
any product. It could be a table, it could be all interior. And that's where it becomes interesting
for me because it's really strong, solid, lightweight, isolating. So we could build a house.

youtube_description:
Dutch designer Eric Klarenbeek talks about the chair made of 3D-printed fungus he showed at Dutch Design Week in 2013.

The technique could be used to create larger, more complex structures such as houses, he believes.

Read the full story here: http://www.dezeen.com/2014/03/06/movie-eric-klarenbeek-mushroom-roots-fungus-3d-printed-chair/
youtube_title: Eric Klarenbeek talks about his chair made of 3D-printed mushrooms
